utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you and to everybody. All the accused are here. Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Defence teams, only Mr. Bourgon absent. I understand there are some preliminaries, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier this morning I sent everybody an e-mail, including your senior legal officer, so I am hopeful that you are familiar with the contents of it. I am ready to start my case, but the evidence which will begin it requires a degree of logistical preparation, and there is still a degree of uncertainty about when we will come to the end of what is ahead of me. And I suppose what I am looking for from you is what in my jurisdiction we would call a time-marking. Where there is, as it were, a bit of a traffic ahead of a trial it's not uncommon for a Court listing officer or a judge to say, Your case will not start before, say, 9.00 Monday morning or 4.00 tomorrow afternoon. I think, with respect, I am not assisted by further information from Mr. Josse or Mr. Vanderpuye. I am really looking for your help so that you can tell me, We want you to start tomorrow, or, We don't think there is any point on that, start Monday morning. And that's really all I've come here today to ask you for so that I can amass my forces accordingly, and I have no doubt that my client would appreciate some certainty in that regard also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Haynes. We will come to that later on after we have heard Mr. Josse, unless he has got some information readily available now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is nothing I can add to what I have previously said. I sent a communication to all counsel in the case today as instructed. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are not aware of that, obviously, because you said you sent it to co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I sent it to all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- all counsel in the case. Your Honour, I am not sure exactly what Mr. McCloskey's stance is in relation to what Mr. Haynes has said save for the fact that there has been some e-mail correspondence between counsel, and he, I think, is probably supportive of Mr. Haynes's position. We certainly are. I don't want to be overly critical of the Prosecution, but the fact of the matter is that when he started cross-examining this witness, Mr. Vanderpuye was asked by Your Honour whether he was still going to be eight hours, and he said considerably less than that. Yesterday, the issue was again addressed just after the second break, and he indicated that he might be a session or two today. The list of exhibits has extended still further, and the Prosecution understandably want information from us, but we are unhappy with the way that they are playing with the time estimate of their cross-examination of this witness which impacts on our decision and even more so on Mr. Haynes's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not open a hole, literally, of unhappiness because you are not the only one who is unhappy, obviously. Mr. McCloskey, supposedly, is also unhappy and so am I. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. They have not followed your order, and I would ask that they -- if you read the e-mail, they continue to hedge. We are very happy to have their expert testify next week. We look forward to cross-examining him. I don't think that their expert should interrupt the testimony of any of the Pandurevic witnesses, and we don't think it should be put off until after that, but we are happy to -- if it takes next week to get the expert here, we are happy to do that. We would like to have a chance to cross-examine that witness. And on the subject of any other potential witnesses that may testify in the Gvero case, I wish that that issue be cleared up while the accused is in court, because that has not been clarified while the accused was in court. The issue is an important issue that if an accused is choosing not to testify that that be clear on the record. It's not clear now because when it was made clear by Mr. Josse, his client was not in court. So, I don't want to be involved in that but I do think, for the record, it does need to be made clear that Mr. Gvero is not testifying. And so both those issues I would hope could be made clear today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I will only comment on the first part of your intervention; namely, that Mr. Josse hasn't complied with what we said yesterday or what we ordered yesterday. I think I made it clear that we were splitting the difference, sort of, between you, and we gave him up to noon -- up to -- sorry, I said noon, what I meant was halfway through the -- today's sitting. My --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, Your Honour -- Your Honour, could I -- let me read out the e-mail. It won't take a moment. This is what I -- was addressed to Mr. McCloskey, it said: "As things stand at the moment, it is not our intention to call General Kovacevic. This present intention is based in part on what was stated during yesterday's proceedings, in particular, that the present witness will be completed today and that after the Gvero opening statement, the Pandurevic case will start tomorrow." Now, I sent that at about the same time that Mr. Haynes sent his e-mail. They crossed. I don't want to put Mr. Haynes in an embarrassing or difficult position because he is not to blame for any of this. That is for certain. And though it's not perhaps a matter for me to comment upon it, I would endorse his request that his client start on Monday. Realistically, we are just asking the Prosecution to finish with this witness, and then we will state categorically what our position is, but they have not been frank, we go that far, we use the word "frank," with how long they are going to take with it. They keep chopping and changing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have heard enough about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are not happy with all this as you may have noticed, however, by majority we have decided to proceed for the time being and reserve our position in due course as we go along. And in the meantime, Mr. Vanderpuye, please, you are enjoined to conclude your cross-examination as soon as possible. Of course, we are not putting any limitations on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to bring in the witness, of course. And, Mr. Haynes, I haven't left your -- the matter raised by you as an unfinished symphony. We will come back to you later on because of course everything depends -- we're talking of Monday. We are all assuming, for argument's sake, that we won't have anything between -- intervening between the end of this gentleman's testimony and your case except for the opening statement of the Gvero Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder whether I could push my luck to this extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I hope you are not expecting me to start today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can safely tell you, Mr. Haynes, that you can start on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am very, very, grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it could well happen that things will move in a way in which it would be impossible for you to start on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's fine. That's really all I was asking for. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. But if things go as anticipated, then yes, you can start on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. General, good afternoon to you. Once more, my apologies for keeping you waiting. You are still testifying under oath and Mr. Vanderpuye will hopefully conclude his cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, yesterday when we left off I was asking you about General Gvero's relationship or -- with international organisations and whether or not he was authorised to maintain contacts with them as the scope of his duties for assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could 65 ter 4156 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It could be put into e-court. It's probably best if the witness takes his earphones off, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, can you kindly take off -- remove your headphones, please. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a new document that deals with Gvero -- alleged Gvero related dealings with the ICRC. Mr. Vanderpuye explained to the Chamber yesterday why this line arises from our cross-examination, and we accept that the Trial Chamber upheld his submissions in this regard. Our observation and objection in effect is this: Why can't he use P536 which is already in evidence to ask the witness about the same area. P536, perhaps that could be put into e-court. That's another document that alleges Gvero's dealings with the ICRC at the same point. In short, why are the Prosecution deliberately choosing to use a new document to conduct this line of cross-examination rather than a piece of evidence that's already been adduced as part of their case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope the answer is not that we haven't got enough documents in the case. What's your reaction or remark, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this document fairly addresses the issue that was raised during the cross-examination of this witness. I think it's appropriate, and I don't know that it's within the purview of the Defence to dictate to the Prosecution which evidence it chooses to use. The Defence has been provided with this document. He evidently is ready and knows what it's about. So it's not an issue of surprise or unfairness with respect to its use. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you intend to prove by this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I intend to show with this document is the role that General Gvero played with respect to his interaction with international organisations. And the reason for that is because it ties to the language of Directive 7, from which the Gvero Defence seeks to distance Mr. Gvero as a potential contributor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And would you have been able to prove the same thing by using P536? There's opportunity to look at it. I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do. I'm looking at it just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think if we can see them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I've repeatedly said, I have no objection to the Court looking and reading both documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in deciding whether there is any substance in the submission I am making, which is, in effect, the Prosecution are deliberately trying to introduce new evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The difficulties are two, Mr. Josse. One is it's not normal that a party is told which documents to use in the course of direct or cross-examination. That's number one. And secondly, we haven't seen either of these two documents. We are seeing one now, and I have asked for the other one to be shown on e-court. And exactly which is P536?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the one to the left is 536. The one to the right is 4156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes, Madam Fauveau, in the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to add one thing to what has been said. The document that the Prosecutor wanted to use, well, we consider that it also has exculpatory elements for our client.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If my learned friend Madam Fauveau is saying that she wants to adduce that document in any event, then there is no point for the Trial Chamber ruling on the submission. Perhaps she could make that clear, and I will withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Fauveau has made that clear. I don't think we should make it clear that the document contains exculpatory material for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour misunderstood. I am simply asking her to make it clear that she wishes it to be adduced. If she does, I will withdraw my objection on that basis, and let's make it clear on the basis that she wants it in and not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- I would just like to clarify that as far as my colleague has alleged or is saying that we can prove the same point by using the same document, that's a separate issue on whether or not we are trying to introduce new evidence because what we are talking about is evidence that is corroborative of evidence that has already been adduced in the case. That's a separate issue than whether it is completely new to the Defence or new to the case. It's not because it bears upon a similar matter but it's corroborative of it, and to that extent, it is appropriate to introduce on cross-examination. And we are not constrained to use the same evidence over and over again for the same witnesses, particularly to the extent that it doesn't raise -- particularly to the extent that it doesn't raise a completely new issue in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Yes, Ms. Fauveau. Do you wish to react to Mr. Josse's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I think I said all that I wish to say for the time being, and I will see during my questioning how exactly I would like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then I pursue my objection on that basis, and Mr. Vanderpuye really said it all, Your Honour. What we submit is what he has just said is not acceptable. That is not a proper way to conduct the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Irrespective and independently of the point raised by Madam Fauveau and what it carries in its wake, our position is unanimous on this. We believe that the Prosecution has every right to use additional documents to make a point, and accordingly we are giving the go-ahead. General -- we don't need the two of them now on the monitor. We only need the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is a document that is issued by the ICRC. It's dated 17 July 1995. And it's an update on ICR activities in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could turn page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The second paragraph of this document reads as follows: "After a meeting held in Belgrade, the European Union envoy Mr. Carl Bildt declared to the media on 16 July that the ICRC would be granted access to all detainees around Bratunac. The ICRC delegates in Pale then had a meeting with General Gvero of the BSA, who ensured them that the ICRC would be given access to all detainees once the security conditions in the area allowed." Now, with respect to that particular conduct, is that consistent with General Gvero's position as the assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs, as a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph can only mean that General Gvero had authorisation from the military authorities to enter into contact with and speak to UNPROFOR and ICRC representatives. Yesterday, I already said something, and I'll repeat what I said, not a single document regulating the responsibilities and functioning of organisational units of the VRS contains provisions that regulate how one should cooperate with the ICRC and so on. The Main Staff of the VRS has its own documents that regulates these matters. They are ad hoc documents. And one can probably come to the conclusion that he had such authority, and as a result, Mr. Carl Bildt evoked the authorisation that he had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These documents that -- these VRS document that contain provisions that regulate cooperation with the ICRC, international organisations, et cetera, did you review those documents prior to preparing your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I examined have been referred to quite precisely. In the report, in the footnotes, you know which ones are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you review those documents in reference to your analysis of General Miletic's role as concerns UNPROFOR, UNHCR or other international organisations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 5 in my report that deals with humanitarian assistance refers to the fact that I examined the decision on cooperation with UNPROFOR and international organisations. Footnote 137, I examined the order of the Main Staff; 138, I examined a document from the Main Staff. And for a period of time I performed a detailed analysis and examined the overall concept, but I thought it wasn't important to include this in the report, but I did state that I had reviewed these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so which one of those documents authorises General Gvero to engage in contact with ICRC, UNPROFOR, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the cooperation remained at the level of General Mladic and General Milovanovic, and then they would authorise him. I'd like to have a look at the document again to refresh my memory about the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 4157.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is also another ICRC document that concerns an interview that was given to Deutsche Welle broadcasting, and it's dated 20 July 1995. In the first part of this document, it reads as follows: "The spokesman of the ICRC Belgrade office Josue Anselmo has stated here today that early this week an oral agreement was reached with General Gvero in Pale, according to which the ICRC delegates are, in principle, authorised to visit the Srebrenica Muslims detained by the BSA when it took over this UN protected area." If we go to the bottom of the page, the paragraph at the bottom of the page reads as follows: "According to Mr. Anselmo, General Gvero agreed with the usual conditions for the ICRC visits to detention centres, which means registration of all detainees, interview carried out in private, giving the detainees the possibility to write Red Cross messages and in this way inform their families that they are alive, repeated visits to the -- repeated visits and the assessment of the conditions of detention." If we go to the next page. In the second sentence it reads: "After the agreement with General Gvero, the ICRC vehicles evacuated two days ago 87 seriously wounded people from Bratunac to Tuzla" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Could my learned friend read the whole of that paragraph, please. Particularly bearing in mind the witness doesn't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will be happy to oblige. It reads as follows from the top of the page: "As for the medical and other assistance, the ICRC delegation was persistently negotiating with medical evacuation -- negotiating medical evacuation of the wounded and sick people who stayed behind on the Bosnian Serb territory in Bratunac and in the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari. After the agreement with General Gvero, the ICRC vehicles evacuated two days ago 87 seriously wounded people from Bratunac to Tuzla. Apart from this, the ICRC teams used their armoured vehicles to transport over 20 people who were unable to walk from the separation lines to Kladanj." Now, in light of what I've read you here as concerns General Gvero's agreement with the ICRC concerning the terms and conditions of access to prisoners, is this something that is consistent with your understanding of General Gvero's role in his capacity as assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a very gratifying task to testify as an expert if the minimum efforts haven't been made, and that would involve translating the entire document that we have here. An expert has to examine all the aspects of a given document. But given what I have heard, there are sufficient arguments for me to provide you with an answer identical to my previous answer. The way things were organised were as follows: This wasn't an integral part of the procedure, but on the basis of subsequent acts and given there were no problems, it's possible to draw the conclusion that such contact was established pursuant to authority received from his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your analysis of the structure and the order of the Main Staff as it was in July 1995, were you aware that General Gvero played such a role with respect to international organisations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having analysed many of the things that were done, I gained a certain impression, the impression that there was a level of organisation, and to an extent UNPROFOR remained in contact with General Mladic and Milovanovic. As far as logistics are concerned, assistants dealt with this. And as far as logistics -- that concerns logistics in the rear, but this area was the responsibility of the assistant for morale, religious, and other affairs. I think this would be part of his field of activity, and as military expert, I would say that as a commander he made very reasonable assessments about those who cooperated with particular organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect particularly to the issue of the conditions of detention for prisoners, is that something that would fall within the sphere of General Gvero's responsibilities or perhaps General Tolimir's responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very difficult to provide you with a precise answer to this question. This opens up the way for speculation. It's a problem for us to answer this precisely because the person who had responsibility didn't make an effort to reconstruct the way in which the VRS was organised. Why am I emphasizing this now? The procedure that concerned prisoners and detainees was the responsibility of the security organ; however, the military prisons in the territory of the former Yugoslavia were regulated in different ways at different stages. So those military prisons that were the responsibility of the organ for legal affairs -- well, they were their responsibility for a certain period of time and then they were the responsibility of the logistics organ for a certain time, and I'm not sure whether the security organ was ever responsible for the prisons. Without determining how things were organised, it's impossible to provide you with a precise answer on responsibility, but it's possible to and easy to reconstruct how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, General, given the -- given the materials that you viewed, it showed General Miletic communicating with UNPROFOR and international organisations, wouldn't it be important for you to know what the duties of other members of the Main Staff were in order to evaluate that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we have in the transcript. Line 11, it says General Miletic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I just wanted to make sure. Thank you. I thought it was but I wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Miletic, line 11. In chapter 5, I stated quite precisely that General Miletic didn't have any responsibility for UNPROFOR, and I said that it was my responsibility to check this, and I also said - and I stated this in the report - that we didn't have an overview of the organisation. When you asked me whether it's normal, well, that's the minimum you should have done before starting on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Paragraph 190 of your report, it says: "Major General Radivoje Miletic participated in decision-making regarding the approval of humanitarian aid and the passage of convoys." Now, with respect to reaching that conclusion, sir, isn't it important for you to know whether or not other Main Staff members had responsibilities as concerns humanitarian aid and the passage of convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The worst thing one can do is take things out of context. Similarly -- well, this question was also put to me in the course of the examination-in-chief, I don't know when exactly, and I referred to Article 191 immediately, and not a single sentence in itself has any meaning taken on its own. And under 191 I stated that the documents that General Miletic signed were information notes that didn't have the character of orders. So 191 explains item 190. As far as examining one's responsibilities are concerned, well, the responsibilities of the organisational units of the Main Staff of the VRS, in many of the items this was examined far more than the responsibility of particular units. I adhered to the subject I had been assigned. If the subject had been broader, I would probably have done what I was referring to a minute ago. I would probably have referred to the organisational development of the VRS and of the ABiH, and then it would have been possible to see where the various parties were at a given point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: To the extent that you actually evaluated the decision-making process regarding the approving of humanitarian aid in the passage of convoys, isn't it important for you to have determined what the relative roles of Main Staff members were with respect to that decision-making process? You can answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not a serious approach if one puts a yes-or-no question to an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I take it that you are refusing to answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, God forbid. I am here at your disposal. I am prepared to answer any question, but you can't instruct me to answer a question by saying yes or no. Experts don't answer questions in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still let's proceed with your answer, please, then, if it goes beyond yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It's not going to be lengthy. I will try and be as brief as possible. When analysing the subject I was assigned, I also examined the way in which humanitarian aid in the Republika Srpska was authorised, and in that analysis -- that concerned the responsibilities of the VRS, in fact, in that analysis I also included an analysis of all forms of humanitarian aid. When I had finished this work and saw that the subject was not the precise subject I had been assigned, well, then, I just went on to draft item 5 where I quite precisely analysed how things worked at the state level, at the army level, and I also analysed how General Miletic was involved in humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 1401 in evidence -- in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is an intercept, as you can see -- well, 1401 B is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could have 1401 B also. I think that's in B/C/S and the General will be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's an intercept that's dated 4th August 1995. It indicates that it was taken by the SDB, State Security Service, Tuzla, CSB. And it's at 1120 hours on 4th of August. Now, if you can see in the title it indicates that this is a conversation between General Miletic and Darko, UN Colonel Quape's translator. This is a conversation that involves General Miletic's approval of certain matters related to the UN forces. And here's what it says. If we go to the middle of the page in the English, it reads: "The colonel says" -- this is D, Darko. "The colonel says that ... that if they are compelled to evacuate the patient by land, you, General, will be responsible for anything that might happen to this severely sick patient as a result of the transport." This is in response the General Miletic's statement where he says: "Impossible, sir. I have attempted to be cooperative with Colonel Quape and in general with all of you. However, the more cooperative someone is with you, the more you take advantage of it. And I no longer wish, until you show that you are as -- that you are as much as you ought to ..." And that's when he gets cut off. What's important about this particular intercept is, if you look at the last part of it, it starts with D. "The Colonel asks if we can please not talk about the past now but about this medivac of this patient, who is in critical condition." The answer to that attributed to General Miletic is: "No, sir, no. The Colonel could have, if he had already made a mistake, and landed the helicopter at," it looks like, "Inzinjering, when he picked those wounded he could have landed at Sarajevo airport, so that we could check on who you were carrying. And I have information that you were not carrying just those two, your wounded. And I have no desire whatsoever to take on any more responsibility myself, because at that time I approved it on my own responsibility, not with the agreement of my commander. I have no desire to take on that responsibility myself, because of your improper behavior." Now, the intercept continues, but before I continue with the intercept I ask you this: With respect to the approval of this medivac process, it's clear here that General Miletic approved this matter on his own accord, and he says explicitly, "without the agreement of my commander." Can you explain how that could be, given your evaluation of what General Miletic's role and responsibilities were with respect to the UN agencies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. In the intercept I -- in the excerpt thereof, you can see that this was a process, an ongoing process, and at one point in time General Miletic was in a place where the -- from which his superior was absent and that -- that was probably the basic command post. I can't tell from the document. Something urgent happened and had to be regulated, and in compliance with all the existing regulations, faced with the urgency, the most senior officer passed the decision as to what to do. That was the only moment when the most superior officer made the decision instead of the commander. This is because of this urgency. In the second part I can see that this urgency, and I repeat it was an urgent matter, this gentleman, a lieutenant whose name I can't remember, again called General Miletic, again put pressure on him, which means that it may be easily concluded that he wanted to introduce some extraordinary procedures to interfere with regular procedures and thus create some problems in the military. The statement that it was easier to cooperate with General Mladic is absolutely normal because he is a man who makes very important decisions, because that is his right. And the statement that he has a better cooperation with General Tolimir is also normal because General Tolimir was the assistant commander or higher-ranking officer, and he had the right to issue different decisions. According to what we have seen in this document, this is a by-the-book example of replacing a superior officer following all the rules and regulations that were in place at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague reminds me that we have a translation of what you said is "replacing," and what I want to know is whether you mean "standing in"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard your colleague and we had the same thing in mind. "Standing in" is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe there is a mistake on the transcript. I don't think the witness has said what is actually written on the transcript. "Standing in." I don't think that matches what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In that case, I think we'll need a further explanation from you, and I would ask the witness to remove his headphones. Madam Fauveau, what did the witness say? If you can avoid using any B/C/S language, please, and speak in French. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the confusion is of -- made between "representing" and "standing in for." In B/C/S, the witness used the term "replacement," to replace, like General Milovanovic who is the Chief of Staff and at the same time deputy commander. The deputy commander is translated with "replace" in B/C/S, which has nothing to do with the term "stand in for."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But then when the question was put to him on line 20 -- lines 20 and 21 of the previous page, he said: "I heard your colleague," that means Mr. McCloskey, "and we had the same thing in mind. Standing in is what I had in mind."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter used the word "standing in" but is not sure that that is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... in B/C/S used the word "replacement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are we agreed on this? Mr. Vanderpuye, do you wish to clarify this matter further?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would prefer for the witness actually to use the word in B/C/S that he used so that it's clear on the record at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and then we will go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put the question myself to him. General, could you please replace your headphones. I take you back a minute or so ago and when you heard Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye exchanging some words and you gave an answer. And you said, "I heard your colleague and we had the same thing in mind." What word did you actually use in your language that you could repeat to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Replacing, "zamijenjivanje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say that you heard my colleague, could you tell us what you heard that you said that you agreed with or you had the same thing in mind? What word did you hear?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your colleague used the Serbian word "zastupa," and then I said that we meant the same thing, not standing in for but replacing, which means that Mr. McCloskey and I understood each other in the Serbian language. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, I seem little bit -- I seem to be a little bit confused and maybe you can clarify it. "Zastupa," in the way that you have used it in your answer, is that the same thing as the other word that you used, which I think was "zamjenik." Is that how you meant it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a very precise person. To my great fortune, I now make a clear distinction among the three words that you used. The first one is a "zastupa," a situation in service. Another one is "zamijenjivanje," that is a moment in time. And the third word is "zamjenik," which is the name of a duty in the Army of Republika Srpska. When I was answering your question very precisely and when I told you what was done by General Miletic about the issue of the helicopter and when I was also very precise and I said that in keeping with the regulations, the textbook example of applying regulations in urgent situations as a person who was replacing the commander probably in the command post, and that's how things ended. Then Mr. McCloskey addressed you and used the word "zastupa," "zastupa," probably wanting us to make a distinction between the two things. Then I told him that I understood what he said, that we meant the same thing, that we were not saying the same thing, and I was using the word "zaminjevete" [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes it's "replacing."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and this is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to another area. During your direct examination you were shown Directive number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could have that in e-court, please, that's 65 ter 29, 29. And if we could just go to page 5 in the English, and I believe it is page 11 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. At the bottom of the page in the English you can see the tasks that were assigned to the Drina Corps, and I think you see that at the top or the middle of the page in the B/C/S, or top as it seems to be. You were asked some questions concerning paragraph marked D, Drina Corps, where it says: "From its present positions its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population." Do you recall being asked questions about that on your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked questions about the part of this directive as concerns the tasks of the Drina Corps where it says: "To inflict the heaviest possible losses on of him," meaning the enemy, "and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I remember the whole thing, now you have read to me only 50 percent of the task of the Drina Corps. Based on only 50 percent of a corps' task, I never provide my answer. I believe that at that moment I insist on -- on my answer as a whole and now I don't know what to say. I think it would be good for you to read the whole task and then ask whatever you think you should ask because in the Serbian language it's rather illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not an objection. It's that recently we have found another copy of Directive 4. I have informed the Prosecutor about this. Perhaps the witness would like to look at the hard copy of this version which is much more legible and which in addition bears the signature of the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am fine with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, if I may correct the transcript. On page 26, line 1, what I said precisely was "Signature of the person who signed it." I did not say it was the author of the document I just said it was the person who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, I guess you are able to read what's written under section 5(d) of this document now. Does that refresh your recollection as to whether or not you were asked questions about it by my learned colleague during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the paragraph. I don't -- I'm not really keen on trying to remember what I said. Either you quote it back to me -- it's very difficult for me to remember every answer of mine, and now it seems that you are actually putting my memory to a test, which is not at all pleasant, is it? So can you please read my answer back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Rather than dwell on the issue, let me just ask you: As you've read this paragraph (d), which is the task that is assigned to the Drina Corps, does this have anything to do with the movement of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I am reading this paragraph (d) carefully - and I've read it already several times - my first opinion would be that this is a very awkwardly worded paragraph, but one can conclude very clearly based on the context that for those who lay down their arms, there would be no problem because there is a very unusual sentence in the middle, "First offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender," and so on and so forth. It may be concluded based on that that the objective of the Drina Corps was the troops or armed men in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware that Momcilo Krajisnik testified in this case on 3rd June 2008?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware in respect of this specific provision he was put the following question: "Now, just very quickly" -- and this was on the transcript of this day, it's at page 21656. I won't read the whole question but I'll read part of the question and the answer. It's between lines 4 and 13: "Now just very quickly you discussed this order in your trial, and in a question -- and you agreed that this language was an order for ethnic cleansing; correct?" "A. Yes." And he qualifies the answer and continues. Do you agree that this is essentially an order for ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer? Is that a question put to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is a question put to you. I'm sorry, I see that it appears in quotes. My question to you is: Do you agree that this is essentially an order for ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, extracting such an order from its context creates some preconditions which you tried to impose on me from the outset and that is bias, and an expert is never biased. If they did not participate in the event they can only answer questions and the answers can just be, I don't know, or I do know. If I were to assess this task as a soldier, despite of the fact that I know who the signatory of the document is, that person would be given a negative mark because when you start by saying one thing and then saying how to do it in a different way, it's impossible from the military point of view. Here a reference is made to disarming, an offer to lay down weapons which does not point to any sort of ethnic cleansing to me. And now, whether I or you have understood the sentence properly may be answered when you look at all the documents of the Drina Corps and its units which were created based on this task. All the rest would be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's your expert opinion, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were actually discussing whether we should have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. Yes. I'd invite that, bearing in mind what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So let's have a break now rather than in six minutes time. 25 minutes please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I have 65 ter 3029 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While that document is getting loaded, General, I had asked you whether your conclusion with respect to Directive 4 as concerns its language referring to -- referring to exhausting the enemy and forcing him to leave Birac, Zepa, Gorazde, those areas together with the Muslim population, in your view, constituted ethnic cleansing, you had indicated that that would be speculative and that you didn't see any language to that effect; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the whole. I said that the level of literacy of the person who drafted this sentence -- well, perhaps this person was exceptionally intelligent but not very literate. One should check these things in depth. I said -- you asked me whether this was my professional opinion and then there was a break so I didn't answer that question. But I feel the need to tell you that I am under oath, I am an expert, I am not expressing the opinions of a layperson and all the opinions I have expressed were expressed in a structured manner, and I told you how this could be checked and how you could reach a different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at 65 ter 3029. I think it should be up in e-court, now, and let me refer you specifically to item 1. This is a Drina Corps document. It is signed by Milenko Zivanovic as commander, and it is dated 24th November 1992, and it refers to number 02/3 of 19 November 1992, Directive 4. And in item 1 it reads as follows: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." Now, it is obvious to you, is it not, that this language comes straight out of Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you quite clear about the nature of what you have just read out to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is the translation that we have. Let me refer you specifically to the language that I'm -- that I'd like to focus you on and that has to do with "... forcing the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I asked and I know why. And what I have already repeated on a number of occasions, Your Honours, is as follows. You can't take combat documents out of context. You can't read through a decision and then interpret the decision as a task. This document for further action, this decision, is the result of the task. This is the decision that the Drina Corps command drafted. In my opinion it's very poor. We have to see what the nature of the task is, the following item. The decision in itself doesn't mean anything because the commander is assigning a task to his subordinates, a task that they carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your view, this task has nothing to do with Directive 4; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion this is not a task, it's a decision. The Drina Corps commander fully understood the task assigned to him by the Main Staff, and the decision was poorly drafted by him. The decision such as it is here has been -- has been very poorly drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, can I ask you something. You tried to distinguish the task itself and the result of the task. What did you mean by the result of the task? Did you mean the purpose of the -- purpose of the operation? What's the result of the task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that question, Your Honour. Perhaps it's a translation problem. I will be very precise. When the commander of a unit is assigned a task by a superior unit, having examined the nature of the task as the most responsible officer, he follows a certain methodology and takes a decision as to what his entire unit will undertake. This decision is relayed to subordinate bodies and they are assigned tasks. His decision isn't important for the subordinate units; the assigned task is important for the units. The task is the mission that they have to carry out and that he defines for them. I think that the task should be referred to on the following page, somewhere, so I would like to have a look at that too, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine. If we could page forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a good time for us to understand what it means to talk about something in context and what happens when you take something out of context. In Directive 4, I commented on a task. I said that it was very poorly put, that someone who was illiterate had drafted it, but as a member of the military, I analysed the order the words had been put in and I concluded that it didn't contain any elements such as the elements Mr. Vanderpuye is trying to attribute to it. When I read through the first few paragraphs from the Drina Corps commander, well, I must say that I was surprised by the catastrophic nature of the decision. However, when I read through all the objectives, and this is not something we could see in the excerpt, when I saw that reference was made to the surrender, to breaking up the enemy and the term -- the term "cleaning up" is used, and the enemy was in mind, well, it was quite clear to me that the objectives were of a different nature. When I read through the task assigned to the 1st Zvornik Brigade, and this task doesn't contain any of these elements I have mentioned, well, having done that, it's clear its unit can't and won't carry out what Mr. Vanderpuye is trying to say is involved in the task. This is an analysis of the entire directive up until this subsequent section. It would also be good to have a look at the order from the battalion commander or, rather, from the battalion -- from the brigade commander to see how this matter was further dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, why would this decision be catastrophic in any respect? I am just asking because that's the translation we received.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be catastrophic because it doesn't reflect the objectives set forth in the best possible way. It doesn't reflect the task that has to be carried out. I gained the impression that the author - and this is a decision from the corps commander - I gained the impression that the person who drafted this wasn't taking into account the order in which things should be done, and this isn't subject of military examinations. So the tasks are a lot clearer. The objectives are a lot clearer. The task is very precise. So it's a curious mixture here. But the task assigned to subordinate units is important for me because it's the units that implement Directive 6. Not you, not myself, nor does this depend on how someone else understands the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have a reference in the transcript to Directive 6. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I had Directive number 4 in mind. I apologise. That's the context that we are discussing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it you disagree, then, with the testimony of one Milenko Lazic who was put -- was shown this particular passage from directive number -- from this particular order and who said it was obvious that it came from the directive? That's at transcript page 21831, lines 3 through 8. You disagree with that opinion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to Mr. Lazic, this Colonel, and you think he was in the Drina Corps, he had a certain position there, I'm not quite sure what the position was, and if he expressed this position on the basis of an extract, well, I haven't heard his testimony. I haven't heard what he said, but if that's what he said, then this only proves that he didn't have a look at the entire context of everything and he poorly understood the task assigned under Directive number 4. And it is my impression that, in this way, he wanted in a certain manner to rehabilitate the poor decision of his superior, and he didn't really see that in the objectives and tasks assigned to subordinate units that things were a lot clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 4147, please, in e-court. This is another document from the command of the Drina Corps. It's dated 14 March 1993. It's entitled, "A combat order for further -- on further action."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what I would like to do is I'd like to refer you first to item number 1 which reads: "Following the successful attacks by the corps forces, the enemy forces suffered heavy losses, especially in personnel, in the general areas of Srebrenica, Skelani, Bratunac, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje. They also lost much of the territory they held before the start of the attacks." If we go down to the third paragraph, it reads: "However, respectable enemy forces are still located in Pobudje, Hrncici, Potocari, Srebrenica, and Osmace. According to available information we believe that there are some 1500 to 2.000 Ustashas in the area of Pobudje, Kravica and Glogova, and about 5.000 armed Ustashas in the general area of Srebrenica and Osmace on. "In addition to armed Ustashas in these areas, according to available information, there are large numbers of unarmed persons, about 30.000 of them in the Srebrenica area and about -- and 25.000 to 30.000 in the Zepa area." Did you have an opportunity to review this document in preparing your expert report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it but I didn't analyse it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind, having reviewed this document, that these 30.000 civilians in the -- 30.000 unarmed persons, I should say because that's what the document reads, in Srebrenica area and 25.000 to 30.000 in the Zepa area, were the result of combat operations conducted pursuant to Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. There is something that I didn't understand. Here it says that in the areas, according to the information available, there are about 30.000 or, rather, 25.000 and 30.000 individuals in Zepa. Are you asking whether this was the result of combat operations and the result of Directive 4, something like that? I am not quite clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your expert opinion, General, these 30.000 unarmed people that are referred to in this document that are in the area of Srebrenica, was that the result of the campaigns that were undertaken after or pursuant to Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single concrete operation can be undertaken based on a directive. This has been told you to a million times. You know it only too well but you keep on repeating this. A directive is a general document. It's a guiding document, a directional document. In order to have a concrete task you have to have an order. So if I were to rephrase your question, the question should read as follows: Is this a result of the order which was draft based on Directive 4, and then it would be a militarily sensible and reasonable question that might yield an answer that you are striving for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Since you posed it, why don't you answer it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we change places? What you have asked me just now, the answer cannot be such from what you said because that question could be termed -- well, I am a soldier -- oh, let's say it would be speculation. Based on Directive 4, which was a directive for the activities of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Drina Corps had its orders that it implemented with its own orders in carrying out combat operations. In one zone of those operations, under item 1, we can see "estimate," which is rather probable as they say, that there are some six -- 65000 to 70000 combatants and that in two places there are -- actually, in one place there's about 30 and in another place about 25.000 to 30.000 inhabitants. The consequence, which is 25.000 to 30.000 inhabitants assessing in context in all the operations, may be such that the units that are listed through the combatants took the population with them and that population was their shield, they dragged them along, which is a very common occurrence. Therefore, what I am saying now is only what is probable. In order to assess the position that you incorporated into your question, or that I incorporated into mine, one would have to analyse the situation in much more detail. However, based on what I analyse, my position is much closer to the truth than yours, which means that the masses of population were the -- a consequence of the armed activities of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could 65 ter 4148 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another document. It is typed signed Milenko Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps. It's dated 13 April 1993. It is addressed to the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska morale, religious, and legal affairs section, and I direct your attention to the second sentence which refers to or reads as follows: "You are well aware that a large number of civilians from Srebrenica and other locations have found refuge in Srebrenica." Now having -- first of all, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you showed it to me yesterday, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having had an opportunity to review this document, does this document have anything to do with the campaigns that were conducted following Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document obviously analyses causes and consequences within Directive 4. This is correct. However, what I said a while ago -- little while ago, stands in connection with this document. You are trying as hard as you can to prove that Directive 4 was an organised expulsion of the population, and I am putting entirely different arguments to you. I don't want to use excerpts for a single moment. What I want to use is the whole. It is true that active -- the enemy forces in Srebrenica are in a very difficult position due to our active operations. It is true that in Srebrenica there are a lot of civilians from Srebrenica and from elsewhere, from the places from which they were expelled. The question is how they found themselves there. This is a question that you are trying to define through this as an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're the expert. What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I expected. This is what you should be asking me. My answer here is that you are well aware of the fact that in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina the population mostly followed their respective militaries and very often they followed their own military in such a way that the military very often or sometimes could not discourage it. They were persistent. And also you know that in some cases, such as the cases of protected areas, the militaries used the population there as their shield, as their logistical support, and as an ambiance from which they were in the position to carry out other campaigns. Bearing in mind the context, and I am very familiar with the context from its very beginning to its very end, in my view after the combat activities in 1992 and the problems that were created by the 8th OG in that part of the front line, after the major counter-offensives the 8th OG was scaring its population. It was dragging the population with them and turned them into a shield. That's how the masses of population were created. This is best seen from the fact that not for single moment they allowed the population to abandon these desperate situations in which they found themselves. And this would be my complex answer in my capacity as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could 65 ter 486, please, in e-court, please. I think we need to go to page 7 of the document. One more page, please. And if we could focus in on section E.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is a document that was published by the Economic and Social Council of the United Nations. It's dated 5 May 1993. And the section you have before you, Section E, under paragraph 30 and 31, it reads as follows: "In early March the estimated population of the enclave of Srebrenica including the surrounding villages was 60.000, about half of whom were said to be in the town itself. The pre-war population of the town was estimated at about 7.000. The enclave had been under siege for 11 months. No humanitarian aid has been allowed in by Serb forces since 11 December 1992. "Forcibly displaced people arrived in three ways, coinciding with offensives by Serb forces from Vlasenica; then from Cerska/Kamenica/Konjevic Polje; and finally from Osmace, Zeleni Jadar, and other villages to the south of Srebrenica. It is estimated that 25.000 to 30.000 people arrived in Srebrenica from the Cerska area alone. In addition, as the Srebrenica enclave itself fell to Serb forces, many more people arrived throughout March and April." First, have you had an opportunity to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then I take it you disagree with the factual accounting that is given with respect to the population of Srebrenica in and around March and April of 1995 -- 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How can this witness deal with that, I ask? And secondly, are the Prosecution really inviting the opening up of this complicated and difficult factual area of this case to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No. I think it's a very straightforward issue in respect of the witness's comments concerning the language of Directive 4 and the other documents that I've shown him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I need to consult with my clients on this; however, I would like to ask you -- with my colleagues, sorry, with my colleagues. I'm sorry. However, I would like to ask you a question and it's a matter of syllogism more than anything else. First you asked him whether he had an opportunity to see this document before, and his answer was "No." Then your question is: "Then I take it you disagree with the factual account that is given ..." et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. How can the conclusion be what you are suggesting if his answer was, No, I have never seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're right as a grammatical error -- as a grammatical issue. The question only stems from his previous answers. Whether he's seen the document or not, the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand -- I understand you better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are understanding the issue as follows: You put a part, an extract from a document to the witness specifically asking him whether he had read or he had come across this document before. His answer was "No." Now, he has read paragraph 30 of this document and you also referred him, if I remember well, to paragraph 31, provided you detach your -- and this is how we have understood your question now once you have explained it. Provided you detach this -- detach your question completely from the events which this paragraph specifically refers to in a time -- in a time-frame, that is the events in 1992 and 1993, then you can ask a general question. In other words, whether the witness agrees or disagrees with displacement that this extract seems to point at or point to. I don't know if I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think so and I'll try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In other words, if he hasn't read this document, I don't think there is any point in asking him specifically on those particular events. But those particular events seem or are meant to indicate a pattern of events, and you can ask on that pattern of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having had an opportunity to hear both what Mr. President has said and having had an opportunity to hear what is written in this article, are you aware of the circumstances that are actually related in this article concerning the civilian population in Srebrenica and their relationship to the Cerska/Kamenica/Konjevic Polje and Vlasenica areas as concerns campaigns that were conducted that resulted in their displacement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second question was much more understandable. Although the first question that you asked was very leading; you expected me not to agree with the figure because it seems that you perceive me as a representative of just one side. And I am going to repeat once again, I am an expert and my expert report is based on professional reliability and neutrality, and I based that on the fact that I was not a participant in the events and there is nothing for me to hide. As far as this document is concerned, in the interpretation something was interesting, a sentence there, and that is that the Serbian forces have entered an enclave and they have -- that the enclave had been under siege for several months. This is how I heard it and I would like you to either confirm it or dispel or -- this is what was translated to me. The way I understood it or the way I noted the sentence -- the sentence was that the enclave fell into the hands of the Serbian forces. This is how I understood and noted the sentence as you were reading and as it was interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to give answer or do you want know read this all back to you again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this sentence in all that? This is what I want to know from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The sentence you may be referring to is: "In addition, as the Srebrenica enclave itself fell to Serb forces, many more people arrived throughout March and April." Is that what you -- is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that enable you to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This enables me not to understand the document. When was it that on the 5th of May, 1993, the enclave fell into the hands of the Serb forces. This is how you read the sentence back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Since you are unable to answer the question, we will just move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I can answer the question. And please, do not speculate about my abilities or inabilities to do something. I put some sub-questions to you in order to arrive at a clear question from you. Let's put it very simply. I read in great detail the report of the Secretary-General of the United Nations and now I've seen this text that is in front of me and I've seen many other texts. I did not analyse them for my expert report because this is the area that had nothing to do with the expert report, and opening the area would require a completely different approach to the exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, we have been very patient throughout, but you've gradually taken on a habit of reacting to the questions put to you in a way which goes beyond answering the question and criticizing Mr. Vanderpuye for asking you some questions. You need to stop this. Mr. Vanderpuye here is doing his duty like everyone else. He's got the right to put questions to you. If he puts questions which are not proper, we ourselves will stop him. Otherwise, please refrain from commenting on whether he should or shouldn't ask you such questions or that -- criticizing the way that the questions are being put to you. I hope I have made myself clear because ultimately we will need -- okay, in other words, for example, you have no right to tell Mr. Vanderpuye, You asked me a leading question. He has got every right to put a leading question to you. So stick to answering the question and nothing beyond that, please. Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry. But of course if the witness can't answer the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's another matter, obviously. He can refer to us and we can protect the witness, as we have done before with every other witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, would you like me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question was having heard an opportunity to hear both what Mr. President had said and having an had an opportunity to hear what is written in the article, are you aware of the circumstances that are actually related in this article concerning the civilian population in Srebrenica and their relationship to the Cerska/Kamenica/Konjevic Polje and Vlasenica areas as concerns campaigns that were conducted that resulted in their displacement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the campaigns that were conducted over a long period of time in that area. I did not recognise in those campaigns in that area what you have just mentioned, which is a displacement campaign or a campaign to displace people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page -- I think it's page 13 of this same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's dated 5 -- 5 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5th May. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We need to go to paragraph 86. It should be about five pages up. That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'm just going to read to you the conclusion, paragraph 87. In that paragraph it reads as follows: "Massive and repeated violations of the Geneva Convention of 1949 were perpetrated in recent combat in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were carried out by Serb forces in Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica in attacking and ambushing civilians attempting to flee their encirclement; in attacking the villages themselves; in refusing to allow humanitarian aid to enter; in refusing to allow the evacuation of the wounded; in attempting to link the above issues to the independent question of freedom of movement for Serbs in Tuzla." Are you aware of any of the circumstances that are related in this part of the conclusion in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The circumstances that prevailed in the area, yes, I am familiar with them. I've perused a number of documents. I've seen a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the combat activities that this refers to, are they in any way related to Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible to tell based on one conclusion of one document extracted from a whole and from combat activities in such a way. Probably it did not arise from that directive. However, even the last thing I said does not have any strong foundations. To put it simply, one cannot expect such an analysis to yield a proper conclusion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am not putting the question to you based on solely this document; I am putting the question to you based upon your expertise outside of what's contained in this document. Do you have knowledge of the circumstances that are mentioned in this document outside of the document, because I know you haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that and the knowledge that I have I listed in my expert report about the combat activities that took place in that area and that are not comprised by this document. For some segments, I even listed the incidents of such combat activities and their frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And based upon your examination of those documents, are you able to say whether or not what I've read to you in this conclusion is in any way related to Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say, but most probably this is not related to Directive 4. Those were regular activities undertaken by the units that were deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will take you to a different area, but related. In your report at paragraph 144, you state that Directive 7/1 validated [sic] Directive 7. Do you acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're a little bit confused. I was a little perturbed by the comment the Presiding Judge made a little while ago. But under 144 I stated the following: Directive 7/1 gives an unnatural order to the Drina Corps. That order was either accidentally or intentionally incorporated, but it was invalidated. So at no point is it confirmed that this task was, in fact, one that had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My colleague has pointed out to me that we have a -- I think a mistranscription in the record. At line 24, my question was that the paragraph stated that Directive 7/1 invalidated Directive 7, not validated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear enough. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be precise once more and say what there is there. Directive 7/1, in practice the order -- the task that the supreme commander gave to the Drina Corps, well, this task was invalidated. I stated quite clearly what had been invalidated or made redundant and what hadn't been invalidated. I never said that Directive 7/1 had been completely annulled, but I did refer to what had been invalidated in Directive 7.
