utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, General. And in fact, what you said was: "In practice, Directive number 7/1 invalidated an unnatural and unacceptable task which the Commander-in-Chief had given to the Drina Corps by Directive 7." And tell us what you mean by an "unnatural and unacceptable task"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the interpreter found it a little difficult to interpret what you said, but I think I understood the interpreter correctly. And in this paragraph 144, I said that the task was unnatural and unacceptable and that Directive 7/1 rendered the task null and void.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What task in Directive 7 was unnatural and unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see Directive 7, please, either on the monitor or could I have the text?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it's 65 ter 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The task to the Drina Corps. That's what I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe that's page 10 in the English. I think it may be page 14 in the B/C/S -- 15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got it up on the screen. It is very precise. This is a directive from the supreme commander. This means it's a document that was issued at the national level, and it was intended for the strategic level in accordance with the directive. At the beginning a task is assigned, and one can clearly see the characteristics of the directive here. It has to do with its general nature and with those it is addressed to. The other elements of this task assigned to the Drina Corps that concerns forces, cooperation, precision, and all these other elements, all of these element are quite precisely defined, and on that basis the commander can create his own decision and assign a task. However, the part of the task that commences with the text, Use every day planned and combat operations to create a climate of insecurity, an intolerable climate, and to make it impossible for people to continue living -- to make it impossible for the population in Srebrenica and Zepa to continue living. Well, I added that this task wasn't a military task. The army doesn't have the forces or the equipment to carry out such a task, and this is why this task is illogical. On the basis of all the facts and on the base of analysis, this meant that the commander of the VRS in Directive 7/1 assigned the Drina Corps a different task, a task that could be carried out in a military manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And paragraph 44 [sic] of your report you say that Directive 7/1 invalidated this particular task that you've referred to regardless of whether that task was inadvertent -- inadvertently or intentionally inserted. Could you tell us how it could be -- a task like that could be inadvertently inserted into this task assigned to the Drina Corps? Under what scenario could that occur?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to tell you because having finished all those military schools that I have mentioned and given all my experience -- well, in light of all that experience, we never had such a scenario. We never had such a case to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give me the para number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is paragraph 144. Maybe I should put it on the e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, transcript said just 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. It's paragraph 144. It's 5D759 is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, I am only using your words, because that's what's in paragraph 144 when you said: "Regardless of whether the task was inadvertently or intentionally inserted ..." What did you mean when you said "inadvertently"? What did you contemplate? What were you thinking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I had in mind -- well, I had in mind what we discussed with regard to Directive 7 for three or four days. How it came to be, I had in mind the illogical elements of the directive. Yesterday I mentioned illogical elements in the directive that had been printed out. I mentioned the illogical nature of the contents of the directive that weren't in accordance with any military documents of any kind and I based myself on that, and I asked myself whether someone wanted to incorporate this somewhere or not, whether it was placed there intentionally or not intentionally, but its place is not there. Such tasks could not be carried out and such tasks were never carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As long as we have Directive 7 up, if we could go to point 6.1. I believe that's 14 in the English; 19 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to refer you to what is, in the English, the third paragraph from the bottom which reads as follows: "The relevant state military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce, and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph can't be seen in the Serbian language on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to go to the next page, page 21. Can you see it now at the top of the page, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you mention this particular provision anywhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report I simply mentioned that item 6.1, in terms of its contents or, rather, item 6 in terms of its contents was not part of the work of the Special Administration for Operations and Training, and then I briefly commented. And I have to find this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to correct the transcript on one point. On page 51, lines 7 through 9, the witness said that point six -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... Special Administration for Operation and Training was not work of the staff and especially of the Administration for Operation and Training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You take that as correct, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't particularly dealt with item 6 in the report; although, I analysed it when preparing to draft the report. If I find it, I will comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that you reviewed a number of documents. Did you not review documents indicating General Miletic's signature with respect to managing or dealing with UNPROFOR convoys, in particular?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my learned colleague please specify the document. If it's the document that I am thinking of, we received it on the 25th of July, far after the report was drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You think actually refer straight to the document straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not referring to a particular document. He said that he reviewed a number of documents with General Miletic's signature on them, and I am asking him whether or not he reviewed any documents indicating any dealings whatsoever General Miletic may have had with UNPROFOR as regards UNPROFOR convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, General, if you could provide us with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer that. Whatever I saw with regard to that matter had the characteristics of information. I think I have mentioned quite explicitly the documents I consulted, and you have it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having reviewed documents that indicate General Miletic's participation in the decision-making regarding the approving of humanitarian aid and the passage of convoys, as you have indicated in paragraph 190 of your report, is there any particular reason why you chose not to quote or expressly analyse the provision of point 6.1 of Directive 7 as I have just put it to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you can see under item 190, well, I answered that question. You can find this in item 191. It's very precisely stated there. Providing security for combat operations is an activity that is not the responsibility of these bodies I mentioned. I didn't analyse this in detail in the written text. I think there was a comment but I examined the order in detail. To understand all the aspects of the order, the similarities to other orders or other directives, the differences, et cetera, and I did this in order to compare it to cases such as this, for example, the hearing or the cross-examination, whatever it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you concede that General Miletic participated in the decision-making regarding the approval of humanitarian aid and passage of convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me read to you what your report says, because maybe you haven't had a chance to look at it in a little while. It says, and I quote: "Major Radivoje -- General -- Major General Radivoje Miletic participated in decision-making regarding the approving of humanitarian aid and the passage of convoys." So that's what you said, General. And that's true, based upon your analysis, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I am asking you to protect me as an expert witness from running around in circles. I am asking you to do this as a human being, as an expert. The link between item 190 and 191 is something that I have discussed at least five or six times in this courtroom, and this matter is being taken out of context again. I'll repeat what I said if necessary. 190 is an item that is explained in item 191, too. This cannot be taken out of context, and I was very precise about that and I am repeating what I have already said, that an information note was never a decision. That wasn't the case in any of the systems in force, whatever one may attempt to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 5D759 in e-court, please. I'm sorry, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue. Let's proceed. 5D759.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is page 85 in the English; page 67 in B/C/S. I think we need to go one page back in the English, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now we have it in e-court so everybody can see what paragraph 100 says, and what it refers to is decision-making. Paragraph 191, that you've repeatedly alluded to, refers to the character of an order concerning the notifications or lack -- lack of such character. What I am asking you about, General, and I'll be explicit about it, is to tell us what you mean when you say "decision-making process" because a decision-making process is not an order. And so paragraph 191 doesn't speak to the question of paragraph 190 in terms of decision-making. So tell us what you mean.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have in mind, what I stated here is something I have shown clearly -- or, rather, I didn't show it, I included it in figure 9. And there it says that the process of the work of the command when taking decisions -- well, it is such that you take the decision, then you relay the decision and you control the implementation of the decision. When relaying the decision, you transfer or relay information, and when you do so, you are participant in that procedure. That's why 191, item 191 related to figure 9 and the process of the working method of the command and it also had to do with how one arrived at the decision. Taking a decision is a complex matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In what manner did General Miletic participant in this decision-making process? What did he do, based upon your expert analysis of the documents you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says and as I have said, he was included in the final stage of the process which involved a process that is well defined here. He signed notifications that did not have the character of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How could a notification about a decision be part of the decision-making, General? How could that be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we have to understand what a decision is. A decision is not a single sentence or a single paragraph. A decision isn't a single document. A decision is a system of documents, of notifications, of reports, and of controls; and when you understand that these are the elements that a decision contains, then you will see that in this process notifications represent an important element of the way the entire procedure functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you're telling us is that he just put it in the mail; is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer, warrant officer, put it in the mail. He relayed the notification, and having signed it, the notification became part of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to look at the documents that are related to Operation Sadejstvo 95?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did have the opportunity to do so and I have said so here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Operation Sadejstvo is specifically referenced in Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to review the work-plan associated with that operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I have an opportunity? I did not understand your question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the work-plan in relation to that operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not have an occasion to get familiar with any work-plans for any of the directives, nor with anything that goes with such documents. If I had had such an occasion, then my expert report would not have the words "probably," "most probably." Judging by all available elements, this should be the case in many of the bullet points of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ask for those documents, General, at any point during the preparation or prior to the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for all the documents that you had, the Defence teams have, the Trial Chambers have, and I was then to classify all the documents consistently with my method of work and with the requirements of my expert report. Among all the documents I was provided with, I did not find any such document in my process of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have in e-court, please, 65 ter 4202.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you should before you is a document entitled, "List of documents of the Sadejstvo 95 offensive operation plan," dated 26 April 1995 and is signed by or submitted by, it reads, Colonel Radivoje Miletic. And what it does is it lists accompanying documents for that plan and it's addressed to the 1st Krajina Corps command. Item 1, lists of documents to the Sadejstvo 95 offensive operation; 2, it lists the Sadejstvo 95 offensive operation plan, graphic representation; then it lists an offensive operation plan text form; at 4, it lists cryptographic data protection documents; 5, order for engineering; 6, order for intelligence support; 7, intelligence support plan; 8, plan of moral and psychological support for the operation; 9, support -- security support plan. What I would like to do is I would like to show you first number 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would be 65 ter 4204.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Under item 1.1(b) we will see that it reads: "By conducting Operation Sadejstvo 95, improve the VRS operational and strategic position, shorten the front line, liberate the forces for maneuver thus creating realistic conditions for the full performance of tasks from Directive number 7." Does that suggest to you, sir, that Directive 7/1 did not invalidate the tasks in Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that it invalidated the tasks. I never wrote that it invalidated the tasks. I was precise only in saying that the task given to the Drina Corps originally was subsequently corrected and made null and void. It seems to me that in the textual part of my report I also wrote that some tasks to be given to or that had been given to other corps were never dealt with in this directive because it went without saying that those tasks were being implemented without any further explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There was nothing in Directive 7/1 that says it invalidates or supercedes any tasks that are assigned in Directive 7, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. In order to answer this question one has to understand the essence of command. When the commander of an operational system receives two directives - and you will find that written precisely in my expert report - which are of a general nature, he cannot implement both. And by the nature of his task, the commander will then implement the task that he received last because it sub-surmises all the other things. It is never the case that one unit can carry out two general tasks or two general directives at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you did point out in your report that that related to inconsistent tasks, did you not? The rule applies to inconsistent tasks.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think -- said -- that I wrote this in this way. Let me find it. I think that I wrote what happened -- what happens when the commander receives two -- when he receives two tasks and two directives, what happens then. Then he implements the last directive that he received, and I said that precisely somewhere, and I am now going to find it for you in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While you're looking for that, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am going to ask if I said in e-court, please, 4208 and that relates to the plan for moral and psychological support for the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind this question, I think we'd better take a break now, please, Your Honour, because my client has absented himself again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This shouldn't proceed in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. We will have a break. Anyway, we are only five minutes away from the break. 25 minutes once more please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we had an exhibit in e-court. I have a hard copy of this available to the -- for the expert. Perhaps that might be -- might make it easier for him to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, what you have in front of you is the plan of moral and psychological support for the Operation Sadejstvo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the witness should take his headphones off for a moment. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, too. General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We tried to sort this out during the break. The Prosecution have been very cooperative and have given me what answers that they can. Can we make it clear that we do not at this point accept what has just been said, that this document relates to the operation. What is not in dispute - its a double negative about to come up - I'll -- sorry. Let me start again. It is not in dispute that this document does not mention Sadejstvo; in other words, it does not mention Sadejstvo 95. There is no question about that. And there is no date upon it, I am also told. So the proposition in the question is not accepted. How we should proceed from here is perhaps a matter for the Prosecution. I accept they are entitled to ask the witness about it, but they need to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. No, please respond to -- no, because I saw you looking at the General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just checking to see if his headphones were on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we have had an opportunity to review these documents and we've spoken with Mr. Josse and explained to him the circumstances under which the particular document I am putting to the witness was arrived at. We have a good faith basis for the question that I've put to the witness because this document was in a sequence of documents that are directly related to Sadejstvo 95. These documents also match up to the plan that I displayed before the witness immediately before I -- immediately before I put this document on -- in e-court. It was 65 ter 4202, and it listed a series of nine documents that correspond to that plan. It is our position that this is one of those documents. And furthermore, I believe it is certainly within the ken of this expert -- this expert's testimony and experience to be able to comment upon the document, in any event, in terms of its documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and what would your question be to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I actually have several questions for the witness, but what this document does it is it outlines, A, who's responsible -- who is the responsible person for putting together this plan for moral and psychological support for this operation, in our view which is Sadejstvo, but any operation, for example, and in particular, issues relating to what those responsibilities are. For example, and I can tell you quite candidly, the document talks about consideration for the plan of moral and psychological support for the operation, the role and tasks of the person responsible for its implementation, and then it will indicate -- in this case, it indicates the commander -- assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs. It talks about informing the public of combat operations of the VRS, and it talks about the types of activities that are associated with that. It talks about psychological and propaganda activities aimed at the enemy, which was the subject directly, I think, of 6.1 in Directive 7, and it talks about the means and the process involved in that. And so these are the questions that I intend to put to the witness in respect of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Again we are perfectly in agreement here. We have taken note of your comment for the record, Mr. Josse. I suppose Mr. Vanderpuye has done the same. Otherwise, the question is perfectly legitimate. I suppose you also need to put to the witness that according to the Prosecution this is a document that refers to -- but that's according to the Prosecution, so ultimately he can come up immediately with telling you, No, I don't agree. So that's the position. Go ahead. General. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, what you have before you is the plan of moral and psychological support for the operation that the Prosecution believes to be Sadejstvo 1995, Sadejstvo 95. And I want to put some questions to you in particular with respect to what is designated as the functions and the responsibilities as concerns this plan. If we look at item number 1, we can see that item number 1, subject, it says: "Consideration of the plan of moral and psychological support for the operation, the role and tasks of the persons responsible for its implementation." Here -- and you can see under column 5 that that designates the assistant commander for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs. That would be correct; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may I would like to say that from the previous session I am still due to present a point from my expert report. You said that while I was looking for that point you would prepare this document that you are now showing to me. If that is no longer of importance, then I suppose I don't have to show it to you. At least that's how we left it off. I don't know what to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're referring to the issue of which do you follow, the directive or the subsequent order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question was about how to proceed when two directives arrive, and when I said that I defined this very precisely in my expert report, your reply to that was, While you are searching for that point, I am going to prepare something else. I believe that now is the right moment to deal with that point and do away with it, and then to move on to what you are asking me now. Thank you. In point 141 of the directive, which is short therefore I propose that I should read it, so it does not have to appear on the screen. It says very precisely: "Given the fact that part of the task that the supreme commander provided to the Drina Corps is inappropriate in military terms, the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska formally elaborated and basically changed the task previously given to the Drina Corps." It is a well-known position in the army when several orders arrive that are in contradiction, one is duty-bound to carry out the last arriving order. Your Honour, if there was no such precise regulation, a lot of the units would still be carrying out the first task, and whenever they received any subsequent tasks, their answer would be, I am still on my first mission, I can't move on. Such a precise definition of the order and the tasks provides for the execution of tasks and unity of command, and this is the explanation of what happens when two directives arrive. The two directives cannot simultaneously prevail in any of the commands, units or systems of the military. And now I can answer the question that you have just put to me now. First it says "Commander" in column 5, and then, "Assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs." The fact that it says "Commander," although I am not an expert for this part of military activities, this means very precisely that the commander is responsible for all the plans and everything in the units, and for the part after that, the responsible person is the assistant for morale, religious, and legal affairs. As a professional organ that elaborates the matter further. Second of all, a list disappeared from the screen very quickly. As a professional, I am saying that this should contain the code-name why the plan of morale and psychological support for the operation has been drafted. In the right-hand column, it should say either "Sadejstvo" or "Spreca" or anything else. It says here only "Attachment 8" "Attachment 2." What we should see here would be the code-name of the relevant operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So it's correct that the assistant commander for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs should be named as a person responsible for this plan; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's the one who actually drafted the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to item number 3, please. I believe that's the next page of both documents. No -- all right. It's page 1 of the B/C/S. It's page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to item number 3, General, the subject of that is informing the public about VRS, combat readiness, and activities of the unit. And in respect of that subject, the persons designated as responsible are assistants for moral guidance, religious, propaganda and information. Does that correct to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is an erroneously interpreted abbreviation. The abbreviation stands for assistant commanders for morale, religious, and legal affairs. Assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What does CIPPD stand for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This abbreviation may be expanded as Centre for Information and Propaganda, or something to that effect. I really don't know what it means. It is probably a centre, but since I've already told you I never saw the organisational development of the military, I don't know the exact name of this unit, but it may as well be a centre. Centre for Information, Propaganda, and Psychological Activities, but this is only in realm of assumptions. It doesn't have to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to point number 4 -- well, before we leave number 3, I'm sorry. It is correct that the subject, informing the public about VRS combat readiness and activities of the units, is an appropriate subject for this type of a plan, that is, a moral and psychological support plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to highlight something that I've already said several times. I am not an expert on the development of this plan. It has its rules, how it's done. It has the rule of the work dynamics, the exact items that have to be incorporated. The only thing that I, as an expert, had to analyse was the course of combat activities, because I thought that this had been taken from somebody else's competencies, but then I revised that it belonged here. I am not the best suited person to tell you whether this is in the spirit of regulations and whether it comprises everything that it should comprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can the witness take his headphones off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- I am very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, once more. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we endorse those remarks from this witness. We submit that this is a blatant attempt to cross-examine this man on the basis that they are not going to have an opportunity to cross-examine our expert. This document appeared on this list overnight. It wasn't on the list yesterday. It rouses our suspicions as the submissions we have been making as to why we were not anxious to disclose our hand. The witness has said it with no prompting whatsoever from us, and we submit the Court should say to the Prosecution, Ask him about what he knows about, by all means, but not about things which are clearly outside the scope of his expertise as he has just made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness has repeatedly and throughout his report referenced work plans, referenced the process by which directives are developed, referenced the necessity for contributing organs to participate in that process, and in respect of that he has made certain conclusions as to General Miletic's involvement in the drafting of Directive number 7, which is obviously a very central issue. He's also made remarks concerning General Gvero's potential contribution to that instrument. This goes directly to the heart of this witness's ability to put forward expert testimony concerning the work-plans that were followed, the method of work that was employed, the methodology of the work that was followed in the VRS in terms of creating directives and in terms of implementing directives. And so this is an entirely appropriate line of questioning considering also that the basis upon which Mr. Krgovic examined this witness in order to distance General Gvero from any contribution to Directive 7 was based upon the nature and the type of information that 6.1 of that directive calls for, that is, the psychological and moral support section of that document. This goes directly to the heart of what it is that organ is supposed to be doing and whether or not what this document shows is consistent with what appears in Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's your point of view, but on the other hand every witness tells you, "I am not the best suited person to tell you whether this is and it's dispute of regulations and whether it comprises everything that it should comprise." And before that he has also told you, "I am not an expert on the development of this plan, if it has its rules, how it's done." Where do we go from there? The whole thing is that I would expect the witness to say, "I am not qualified to answer this question." And you move to your next question. But he is not doing that, so in other words I am not blaming you, and I can understand also the way the witness is trying to fill up his answers when he is faced with difficult questions like this one. But on the other hand, if he tells us I am not qualified to answer this question, where do you go from there? Shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered you more or less. I don't think under the circumstances you can proceed with the same matter unless you are not satisfied with the truthfulness of his answer in which case you can contest that. But other -- beyond that, I don't think you can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would bear with me for a moment, I would like to confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may address the Court, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness has offered rather extensive testimony on his direct examination and on his cross-examination with respect to these fundamental issues, his concerns, the process -- work process, et cetera, as related to the drafting of directives and implementation of directives and th relative roles of responsibilities of the participants in that work process. He has answered a number of questions that have been put to him by Mr. Krgovic as well as a number of questions that have been put to him by Ms. Fauveau, and you've heard these answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's our position that at this position for this witness to now suddenly claim - and I do mean suddenly claim - that he's not in a position to answer a question about whether or not propaganda aimed at -- aimed at the enemy, for example, is an appropriate subject matter falling within the organ of morale, religious and legal affairs, it is simply not credible. It's not believable and that's the reason why I am continuing to put these questions to this witness. And I think that he has at certain points been cooperative in answering questions; and at other points he's been, frankly, belligerent about answering questions, and I don't -- we don't accept his statement that he's now claiming that he's not an expert in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say this is a bizarre situation because in one sense we agree with Mr. Vanderpuye. We are not asserting that this gentleman's a credible witness, obviously, and those representing Miletic are, and that's understandable, but this is a completely bizarre situation. But if he really takes that view -- the jurisdiction I come from, he should put it to the witness robustly and say, You're -- you're -- this is what you are now doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean there is no more place and space for mixing up submissions and what Mr. Josse has just pointed out now. If, as you put it to us, you are not believing the assertion or the statement made by the witness in reply to your last question, on the basis of what you have explained to us, then you are free to face him with that but be specific and go for the kill, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, keep it as a submission for later. I mean, we are in a perfectly -- in a perfect position to weigh the entire testimony of every witness because we pay attention to what is being stated and what applies to this witness applies to every other witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, you've commented in your report and in your testimony about the work plans that were implemented and followed by the VRS with respect to directives and orders, et cetera. And with respect to that testimony, it's fair to say, given what you've said now, that you are not an expert in that area at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the field of planning?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the field of planning in respect of the report that you generated concerning the contributions that are made by respective organs of the General Staff to the creation of a directive. Main Staff. I'm sorry if I have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem, unless it's a problem for the transcript. Given the material made available and presented to the Tribunal and in my CV and the list of works, you can find among other things my reference to military management or, rather, command. If we try to refresh our memories, the first process in military management or in command is planning. That's my natural activity, and so on that basis that I dealt with development and organisation, and it's on that basis that we dealt with functioning. However, within the context of that planning -- well, this wasn't a sphere of activity for myself or my organs. As an expert, I dealt with the organisation of military hospitals, but I never discussed operations, the method of operating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not happy with the interpretation. I am not happy in the sense I am not criticizing the interpreters. I want to make sure that I have understood what the witness has said or that -- or that what he has said has completely been translated to us. Here I have: "However within the context of that planning -- well, this wasn't a sphere of activity for myself or the organs. As an expert I dealt with the organisation of military hospitals, but I never discussed operations, the method of operating." Is this -- does this reflect completely what you wanted to tell us, General, or what you said? Or do you wish to explain it further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that perfectly reflects what I said. We dealt with the organisation of organs for morale, psychological, legal, and religious affairs. We dealt with the way they were functionally linked up. We dealt with the number of actors they had. We will dealt with the number of responsibilities they had and how they were distinct from others, but I never dealt with the contents of their work itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's his answer, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you never dealt with the contents of their work, how can you exclude, for example, General Gvero as a contributor to 6.1 of Directive 7 based upon its content? How do you do that as an expert, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which example I provided you with and then I can provide you with an precise answer. If I said that it's his sphere of activity, well, it's his. If I said it's his sphere of activity, I am not talking about things were done. Give me an example. Organisation -- or the organs for organisation can locate where certain activities are carried out, but they are not responsible for analysing the quality of the operations carried out, and that's the essential distinction that has to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you said in response to my colleague Mr. Krgovic's question, on page 30244 of this transcript is that: "Not only does it not correspond with this element of support," speaking of this entire paragraph 6.1 of Directive 7. "Not only does it not correspond with this element for support," meaning morale, religious, and legal affairs, "for this kind of support for a combat operation, this entire paragraph is not in keeping with its purpose." That paragraph describes specific actions to be undertaken in relation to the dissemination of information, in relation to contact with international organisations, UNPROFOR, et cetera. You've distinguished that on the basis of its content. I am asking you whether or not you consider yourself sufficiently expert enough to make that kind of a determination when you can't even answer the question about whether or not informing the public about the VRS combat readiness and activities of the units is properly within the organ of -- under General Gvero's command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four questions. I will start with the first one. When I analysed item 6, support for combat operations, well, I was very precise and I said that item 6 has its structure, it's very own structure, and that structure is the element that the organs for planning have to be familiar with. They have to be familiar with item 6 with regard to this element. 6.1 has to do with information, intelligence, self-protection, combat engineering, moral and psychological support, and logistics support. This is elementary information that one has to have to know something about the support for the combat operations. When I read through the item, support for combat operations, then I saw that under moral and psychological support other activities are mentioned, and someone who has a certain elementary knowledge, I said that this isn't in the right place. Not in any case did I -- not in any case did I assess the contents with regard to the material you have referred to. The material you gave me as a retired military expert as someone who has worked on a number of studies, with regard to that material I can provide you with my professional opinion. It's not the opinion of a layman. However, at this point in time I am making a distinction between that opinion and the opinion of an expert, and I believe that for you and your Tribunal, if you want a detailed analysis of the contents you need an expert to deal with these elements, with this element. What I said had to do with the person who was responsible. I said I had no reliable information according to which the plan for the psychological and moral support was part of the Operation Sadejstvo 95 because it has a precise designation. We can discuss things at length. You'll have the appearance of a General, I can present you with the opinions of a General, but not with the opinions of someone who is an expert on this particular matter. I am very precise and very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you are not an expert in being able to determine what properly falls within the jurisdiction or competence of one organ of the Main Staff, how do you propose to be an expert to comment upon what falls within the jurisdiction or competence of another administration, department, whatever you want to call it, of the Main Staff? How do you propose to distinguish between those two aspects in terms of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am under a lot of pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, if you are feeling tired and you wish to stop, we can stop here for today and continue tomorrow. I don't want you to feel -- answer a question -- questions when you feel under pressure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not under that kind of pressure, but I have to accept certain conclusions, certain language, for example, you're an expert, you're not an expert, and so on and so forth, and then I have to answer in a manner that won't irritate you because, above all, I want to make a contribution here. That's my main mission. The question has confused two issues: First of all, the fact that I am an expert, and that has been demonstrated. It has been checked by NATO representatives. Two, I know how to organise and recognise functional responsibilities of all organisational units in an army. But I am not an expert, and this is natural because I don't deal with all matters, I am not an expert in assessing how certain functional responsibilities are carried out in certain organisational units. What I analysed under item 6 had to do with the first domain. I just made a distinction, and this relates to the domain of contents. There is absolutely no dilemma about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you don't know how functional responsibilities are carried out, how can you possibly comment on what it is that General Miletic was doing in July 1995? Because whatever it is he was doing is functional by definition.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a plan for moral and psychological support for the operation before me. I was quite precise about that. The organisational work of the staff, of the command of the operational staff organs is an integral part of every military academy. These are subjects that are dealt with in all military academies, in military academies I went through, and it's part of my duties to deal with this. There's no dilemma about this. As for moral and psychological support, well, I never we went to a school that dealt with this and it's not part of my duty. So let's make a distinction. An expert on organisation, an expert on management, an expert on planning, an expert on human resources, this is what I dealt with, for example, such a person is not by definition, as you would expect, an expert on moral and psychological support, on intelligence support, on logistics support, on finance, or on anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So when you say, for example, that General Miletic's involvement with UNPROFOR in terms of the decision-making process concerning approvals of convoys, you are talking about that from a purely theoretical point of view. You don't know what he actually does or what he's supposed to do, because that would be his functional responsibility and you've told us that you are not an expert in that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. You haven't said that. So I am asking you a pretty basic question about what it is that a person that's assistant commander for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs ought to be doing or what he oversees in terms of a plan for moral and psychological support? And if the answer is "I don't know," just tell us so.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is precise. I know that such a person has to have a plan for moral and psychological support for the operation. As for the contents of the plan, that's not my subject and I am not familiar with the contents of the plan. So I know that such a person has to create a plan, but I don't know what the contents of that plan might be. That's precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the same goes for every other organ in the Main Staff, as far as your knowledge is concerned; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I have to remind you of everything that I have already said and of everything that has been written down and of everything that I have drafted here. Organisation and the functioning, operations and staff duties and human resources, well, these are things that I am an expert on. No one asked me to do any studies that dealt with issues beyond that field. So military management or command, all those processes, organisation, functioning, human resources, I deal with all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In light of the answers that you've given us in response to the questions I've put to you, don't you think it's incumbent upon you to withdraw your answers to what Mr. Krgovic asked you concerning the role of the organ that General Gvero is in charge of, concerning the role of the organ for morale, religious and legal affairs in terms of its contribution to Directive number 7, in particular point 6.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness please be read back the question and the answer. I did not speak about the responsibilities of General Gvero or of his organ. I just had one question whether this was in keeping with the functional powers, whether the parts under the part psychological and moral support are part of the functional competencies. I did not mention any contents or anything. That was the essence and gist of my question, and the witness agreed with that. Could the witness please be read back both my question and his answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Could you direct the witness straight to the questions and answers that you referred to in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Krgovic, and this is again at page 30244, lines 13 through 22: "If you analyse the portion right here, you can see that these elements being introduced, such as logistics, PVO support, things to do with mobilisation, this entire paragraph does not contain anything, at least in my view, that would correspond with moral and psychological support. Not something that would seem to be in keeping with the rules of the military profession; right?" "A. Not only does it not correspond with this element of support for combat operations, this entire paragraph is not in keeping with its purpose. This entire paragraph that relates to support for combat operations and then with the specific emphasis on 6.1." My reference to the contents refers -- is derived directly from Mr. Krgovic's question where he says what the paragraph contains. Given what you responded to Mr. Krgovic's question, do you feel that your answer is sufficiently informed by your expertise?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely believe and I have answered what I just told you a while ago. The powers of a military officer, of a commander is to know what points and sub-points are contained in the support to combat operations. And I answered. Not only does this paragraph not correspond to that, it is not in consistency with the structure that is laid out, and it is not in consistency laid out in the structure because there is a reference to engineers and many other things, and we that the engineer support of combat is a special point. Combat support is a special support. This is what you are being taught in the basic military academy, and I dwelled upon the contents of the structure. I did not analyse. I did not enter the contents of the point that is in that structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 7.00. Shall we stop here? How much longer do you have, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have quite a few numbers -- quite a few areas to cover. I will do my best to cut down what I address with him tomorrow. I -- the problem is, Mr. President, I have not as much control over the situation as I might otherwise because of the nature of the way the witness answers questions and the nature of the way the witness conducts himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's stop here. We will continue tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
